MHHS2401 · Week 4 · Muscle Physiology II — Dr Linda Ban

Muscle tension & performance

Part II picks up where excitation–contraction left off: where the ATP comes from (and why muscles fatigue), what actually sets the force a muscle produces, and how three fibre types — tuned by genetics and training — decide whether you're built to sprint or to last. Built from the lecture, using its own figures.

§0Energy & fatigue · LO1

Fuelling contraction — and fatigue

Three ways to make ATP, chosen by how long and how hard you work.

Contraction is expensive, and a muscle swings between almost no demand at rest and a huge demand during activity. It can't store much ATP, so it must make ATP on the fly — three ways, each a different bargain between speed and yield. This section is LO1: the energy systems, why muscles fatigue, and how they recover.

Where the ATP goes

Before making ATP, note what spends it. Three ATPases run the show:

ATP-dependent processes in muscle
ScenarioEnzymeFunction
ContractionMyosin ATPaseCross-bridge formation and separation (the power stroke and release)
RelaxationCa-ATPasePumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, ending contraction
At restNa-K-ATPaseRestores Na⁺/K⁺ gradients across the membrane so action potentials can keep firing

So ATP is spent even to relax and even at rest — the muscle is never truly free of demand.

§0.1Three ways to make ATP

1 · The phosphagen system is the instant reserve. Phosphate bonds are high-energy, which is why hydrolysing ATP to ADP + phosphate is the body's energy currency. The enzyme creatine kinase (CK) runs a reversible shuttle: at rest it transfers phosphate from surplus ATP onto creatine, banking it as phosphocreatine (PCr); at the onset of activity it strips that phosphate off PCr to regenerate ATP almost instantly. Plate 0.1 shows the CK shuttle.

Label Key — the phosphagen reaction
CP (phosphocreatine)
The stored phosphate bank; donates its phosphate to make ATP fast.
ADP
The spent currency waiting to be recharged.
Creatine kinase
The reversible enzyme — banks phosphate at rest, releases it during activity.
Creatine + ATP
The products during activity: recharged ATP (usable energy) and leftover creatine.
Yield / duration
1 ATP per CP, no O₂, ~15 s — instant but tiny; it only bridges the first seconds.

2 · Anaerobic glycolysis is slower than PCr breakdown but makes twice as much ATP. In the cytoplasm, relying on glucose uptake and glycogenolysis, it yields 2 ATP + pyruvic acid. The pyruvate's fate is the fork in the road: with oxygen it feeds aerobic respiration; without oxygen the excess becomes lactic acid.

3 · Aerobic respiration (oxidative phosphorylation) is slowest — it needs a steady O₂ supply — but by far the most efficient, making ~32 ATP + heat in the mitochondria from glucose and fatty acids. The O₂ comes from myoglobin (stored in muscle) and haemoglobin (delivered by the blood, which depends on ventilation).

Plate 0.2 lines the three systems up against the clock — which fuel powers which phase of exercise.

Label Key — the exercise timeline
~6 s
Stored ATP already in the muscle is used first.
~10 s
ATP is regenerated from creatine phosphate (the phosphagen system).
30–40 s
Muscle glycogen → glucose, oxidised by the anaerobic (glycolytic) pathway.
Hours
Prolonged exercise runs on aerobic breakdown of several nutrient fuels.
The three energy systems compared
SystemWhere / needs O₂?SubstrateATP yieldRate (mol/min)
I · Phosphagen (PCr)Cytoplasm · no O₂Creatine phosphate14 (fastest)
II · Anaerobic glycolysisCytoplasm · no O₂Glucose / glycogen22.5
III · AerobicMitochondria · needs O₂Glucose + fatty acids~321 (slowest)
Reasoning · why three systems, not one

The table is a single trade-off written three ways: speed versus yield. PCr delivers ATP fastest (4 mol/min) but only 1 ATP per molecule and only for seconds — perfect for the explosive first moment. Aerobic respiration is the opposite — a trickle (1 mol/min) but ~32 ATP per glucose, sustainable for hours. Glycolysis sits between. No single system can be both instant and inexhaustible, so the body layers them, handing off from fast-and-small to slow-and-large as an effort lengthens. That hand-off is Plate 0.2.

Memory hook · the hand-off order

Sprint → jog → marathon = PCr → glycolysis → aerobic. Fast fuel first, big fuel last.

Worked example · which system for a 10-second sprint vs a marathon?

Use the yields and rates from the table to reason about two efforts.

  1. The demand: a maximal sprint needs ATP now and only for a few seconds; a marathon needs ATP steadily for hours.
  2. Sprint: the fastest supply wins. PCr delivers at 4 mol/min — highest rate — but runs out in ~15 s. That's exactly a sprint's length, so the phosphagen (then early glycolytic) system dominates. Yield per molecule is irrelevant when the event is over in seconds.
  3. Marathon: rate matters less than total ATP. Aerobic respiration yields ~32 ATP per glucose (vs 2 anaerobically) and never accumulates lactate, so it can run indefinitely — the only system that can.

Answer: sprint → phosphagen/anaerobic (fast, low yield, brief); marathon → aerobic (slow, high yield, sustained). Same muscle, different fuel, chosen by duration.

§0.2Fatigue & recovery

Muscle fatigue is when active skeletal muscle can no longer generate or sustain the required power output. The mechanisms sit at many points along the pathway and are associative rather than causal — grouped into two families:

  • Depletion theories — exhaustion of the metabolic reserves that make ATP: glycogen (for high-intensity) or oxygen (for endurance).
  • Accumulation theories — a build-up of lactate and a fall in pH that impairs enzyme activity (CK, the ATPases) and molecular interactions (e.g. Ca²⁺ binding to troponin).

Recovery is the period afterward where depleted substances are replenished and accumulated ones removed. This is why you keep breathing hard after stopping — repaying the oxygen debt:

  • Alactacid — aerobic respiration makes ATP that restores PCr and refills muscle O₂ stores (myoglobin).
  • Lactacid — aerobic respiration regenerates NAD⁺; lactic acid is converted back to pyruvate → glucose → glycogen.
Clinical / real-world · the oxygen debt you feel

The heavy breathing that continues after a hard sprint isn't wasted — it is the body paying back the oxygen it "borrowed" by running anaerobically. That extra O₂ rebuilds PCr, reloads myoglobin, and clears the lactate by turning it back into glucose. It's the physiological reason a hard effort leaves you puffing at the finish line, and why the fitter (more aerobic) you are, the smaller the debt.

R Recall checklist — energy & fatigue
  • ATPases — myosin (contract), Ca (relax), Na-K (rest).
  • Phosphagen — CK shuttles phosphate; PCr regenerates ATP fast (1 ATP, ~15 s, no O₂).
  • Anaerobic glycolysis — cytoplasm, 2 ATP + pyruvate → lactate without O₂.
  • Aerobic — mitochondria, ~32 ATP + heat, needs O₂ (myoglobin + haemoglobin).
  • Fatigue — depletion (glycogen/O₂) + accumulation (lactate, ↓pH); associative.
  • Recovery — oxygen debt: alactacid (restores PCr) + lactacid (lactate → glycogen).
§1Muscle tension · LO2

What sets muscle tension

Tension is the load a fibre can resist — set by four things, starting with length.

Tension is the force a muscle fibre can resist — i.e. the load it can hold or move. It isn't fixed; it depends on four factors, the four S's: Stretch (sarcomere length + structural proteins), Stimulation (motor units + firing rate — §2), Size (bigger fibre = more tension, and size is trainable), and Stores (enough ATP and enough calcium). This section takes stretch; §2 takes stimulation.

Stretch: sarcomere length

How stretched a sarcomere is before it contracts sets how much force it can make. Plate 1.1 is the classic length–tension curve: there is an optimal resting length (~2.0–2.3 µm) where thin- and thick-filament overlap allows the most cross-bridges, and therefore maximal tension. Stray too short or too long and tension falls away.

Label Key — reading the curve
Peak (~2.0–2.3 µm)
Optimal resting length — ideal thin/thick overlap, maximum cross-bridges, maximum tension.
Decreased length (left, ~1.3 µm)
Filaments over-overlap and collide; fewer productive cross-bridges → low tension.
Increased length (right, ~3.7 µm)
Too little overlap — the filaments barely reach each other → tension approaches zero.
Insets (a)–(e)
Snapshots of thin (red) and thick (blue) filament overlap at each length, explaining the curve's shape.
Reasoning · why overlap is everything

Force is made by cross-bridges — myosin heads pulling on actin. The number that can form depends entirely on how well the two filament sets overlap. At optimal length, almost every head has an actin site to grab. Squash the sarcomere and the thin filaments overlap each other and the thick filaments jam against the Z discs — the geometry fights itself. Stretch it too far and the heads reach into empty space. Tension tracks overlap, and overlap tracks length — which is exactly why a pre-stretch before a jump (or a doctor positioning a joint) changes the force available.

§1.1Structural proteins & Duchenne muscular dystrophy

Contraction would tear a fibre apart if the machinery weren't anchored. Structural proteins hold the contractile proteins to the sarcomere (longitudinal) and the sarcomere to the sarcolemma and extracellular matrix (lateral). Plate 1.2 shows the three:

Label Key — who anchors what
Nebulin
Spans the Z disc along actin; aligns and stabilises the thin (actin) filament.
Titin
Runs from Z disc to the M-line; stabilises myosin, provides elasticity, and transfers force longitudinally — the molecular spring that recentres the sarcomere.
Dystrophin
(Beyond this view) anchors the sarcomere to the sarcolemma via β-actin; stabilises the membrane and transfers force laterally.
M-line / Z disc
The anchor points — M-line at the sarcomere centre, Z discs at its ends.

Dystrophin's lateral anchoring is best seen in Plate 1.3: it links the internal actin cytoskeleton, through a complex of membrane proteins, out to laminin in the extracellular matrix.

Label Key — the lateral tether
Dystrophin
The internal rod linking actin to the membrane complex — the keystone protein lost in DMD.
Dystroglycan / sarcoglycan complexes, sarcospan
Membrane-spanning proteins that pass the force through the sarcolemma.
Laminin
The extracellular-matrix anchor on the outside — the far end of the chain.
Actin filament
The internal cytoskeleton the whole complex holds onto.
Clinical / real-world · Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)

Delete the dystrophin gene and the fibre makes no functional dystrophin — snapping the lateral tether in Plate 1.3. It's X-linked recessive (~1 in 5000 live male births). Without the anchor the sarcolemma is destabilised: fibres become fragile and rupture with normal use, triggering inflammation and scarring. Clinically that means progressive muscle weakness, a characteristic Duchenne gait heading toward wheelchair dependence, and — because the diaphragm and heart are muscle too — reduced cardiorespiratory function. It is the textbook demonstration that structural proteins aren't scaffolding trivia: lose one and the muscle literally tears itself apart.

Memory hook · the four S's & the three anchors

Tension = Stretch · Stimulation · Size · Stores. Anchors: Nebulin=aNctin, Titin=my-T-osin (spring), Dystrophin=sarcolemma (the DMD one).

R Recall checklist — muscle tension
  • Tension = load a fibre resists; set by the 4 S's (Stretch, Stimulation, Size, Stores).
  • Length–tension — max tension at optimal length (~2.0–2.3 µm); too short/long ⇒ less overlap ⇒ less force.
  • Nebulin stabilises actin; titin stabilises myosin + elasticity (longitudinal); dystrophin anchors to sarcolemma (lateral).
  • DMD — no dystrophin (X-linked recessive) ⇒ fragile sarcolemma, weakness, reduced cardiorespiratory function.
§2Stimulation & tone · LO2

Stimulation, twitches & tone

The other lever on tension: how many units you recruit, and how fast you fire them.

Stretch sets the ceiling; stimulation decides how close you get to it. Two dials: how many motor units are recruited (and how big), and how fast they fire. Together they scale a single twitch all the way up to sustained maximal force.

Motor units — the recruitment dial

A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres its axon branches innervate. Plate 2.1 shows one running from the spinal cord to its fibres. Tension is graded by recruiting more motor units and larger ones; and a sustained contraction needs a continuous stream of action potentials from neuron to muscle.

Label Key — the motor unit
Somatic motor neuron
The single neuron (cell body in the spinal cord) whose axon branches define the unit.
Neuromuscular junction
Where each axon branch meets a muscle fibre and passes on the action potential.
Muscle fibres (cells)
All the fibres one neuron controls — they contract together, as a unit.
Two colours
Two separate motor units interleaved in the same muscle — recruit more of them for more force.

Rate of impulses — twitch, treppe, summation

A twitch is one round of excitation, contraction and relaxation in a fibre. Fire them faster and tension builds in stages (Plate 2.2):

  • Treppe (staircase) — at the onset of contraction, successive twitches climb in tension, possibly because calcium re-uptake by the SR lags behind.
  • Wave summation — as twitch frequency rises, fibres can't fully relax between stimuli, so tension from successive twitches partially adds.
Label Key — building tension
(a) Single twitches
Widely spaced stimuli — the fibre relaxes completely between each; tension returns to zero.
(b) Summation
Stimuli arrive before full relaxation, so twitches partially add — the tension baseline climbs.
Stimulus marks (▲)
Each triangle is one stimulus; closer triangles ⇒ more summation.

Push the frequency higher still and you reach tetanus — twitches so rapid they fuse (Plate 2.3). Unfused tetanus still shows slight relaxation between stimuli; complete tetanus is a smooth, steady maximum. If the muscle fatigues, tension falls despite the stimuli continuing.

Label Key — fusing the twitches
(c) Unfused tetanus
Stimuli still just far enough apart for slight relaxation — a bumpy plateau below true maximum.
(d) Complete tetanus
Twitches fully fused into a smooth, steady maximal tension.
Fatigue
Even with stimuli continuing, tension eventually falls as the muscle fatigues.
Single-twitch line
The tension of one twitch — the baseline all this summation builds above.
Reasoning · why faster firing makes more force

A single twitch releases a pulse of Ca²⁺ that the SR immediately starts pumping back — so the fibre relaxes before it has developed full force. Fire again before the Ca²⁺ is cleared and the cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ stacks up: more troponin stays occupied, more cross-bridges keep cycling, and the tension of each twitch adds onto the last. Keep firing fast enough and Ca²⁺ never falls — the fibre never relaxes — giving the smooth maximum of complete tetanus. Tension is really a story about how long calcium stays elevated.

Clinical / real-world · motor neuron disease (MND)

If the neurons themselves degenerate, stimulation fails and twitches become fewer or aberrant. MND is the death of the neurons controlling skeletal muscle (~10% familial, 90% sporadic). Lower motor neuron loss cuts excitation directly; upper motor neuron loss removes inhibitory control of the lower neurons. ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), the commonest form, hits both. The result is muscle atrophy, weakness, reduced respiratory function and impaired speech — a disease of the "stimulation" dial, mirroring how DMD (§1.1) was a disease of the structural anchors.

Muscle tone

Muscle tone is muscle tension at rest — what keeps you upright and your head balanced. It's produced by low-frequency twitches giving a weak, sustained contraction, controlled by the CNS (voluntary) and by muscle reflexes (involuntary). Disorders sit either side of normal:

Disorders of muscle tone
ToneFeaturesExamples
HypotoniaLoss of tone, flaccidityLower MND / ALS, myasthenia gravis, DMD
HypertoniaIncreased tone, spasticityUpper MND, tetanus

Prolonged hypertonia can lead to contracture — a permanent shortening of the muscle.

§2.1Types of contraction

Not every contraction moves a load. Plate 2.4 demonstrates the two families with a book:

Label Key — the three demonstrated
(a) Concentric (isotonic)
Muscle shortens to lift the book — tension constant, length falls.
(b) Eccentric (isotonic)
Muscle lengthens under control to lower the book — tension constant, length rises.
(c) Isometric
Muscle holds the book steady — tension constant length, no movement.
Isometric vs isotonic — zoomed out and in
IsometricIsotonic
DefinitionMuscle length is constantMuscle tension is constant (concentric = shorten, eccentric = lengthen)
FunctionHold an objectMove an object
Contractile proteinsSome cross-bridges formMore cross-bridges cause the muscle to shorten (or reverse)
Structural proteinsElastic proteins stretch to compensate (no length change)Elastic proteins fully stretched

Plate 2.5 shows why length can stay constant even as cross-bridges pull: the elastic elements (titin) take up the slack.

Label Key — constant length, shortening inside
Sarcomeres
The contractile units — they shorten as cross-bridges cycle.
Elastic element
The series spring (titin/tendon) that stretches to absorb that shortening.
Muscle length
Stays constant overall (isometric) because the spring lengthens by exactly what the sarcomeres shorten.
Memory hook · iso-what?

Iso-metric = same metre (length) → hold. Iso-tonic = same tone (tension) → move. ConCentric = Closes/shortens; Eccentric = Extends/lengthens.

R Recall checklist — stimulation & tone
  • Motor unit — one neuron + all its fibres; grade force by recruiting more/larger units.
  • Twitch → treppe → summation → tetanus — faster firing, less relaxation, Ca²⁺ stays up, tension climbs.
  • Tetanus — unfused (slight relaxation) → complete (smooth max); fatigue drops it.
  • Tone — resting tension from low-freq twitches; hypotonia (flaccid) vs hypertonia (spastic → contracture).
  • MND/ALS — degeneration of motor neurons ⇒ atrophy, weakness, respiratory/speech impairment.
  • Isometric = constant length (hold); isotonic = constant tension (move: concentric/eccentric).
§3Fibre types · LO3

Fibre types & performance

Three fibre types, tuned by genes and training — sprinter or marathoner.

Not all skeletal muscle fibres are alike. Three types trade speed against endurance, and their structure follows exactly from the energy systems of §0. Which mix you have is mostly genetic; what you do with it is training.

The three skeletal muscle fibre types
CharacteristicType I
Slow oxidative		Type IIa
Fast oxidative-glycolytic		Type IIb
Fast glycolytic
Contraction speedSlowFastFast
Myosin ATPaseSlowFastFast
Main ATP pathwayAerobicAerobic (+ some anaerobic)Anaerobic glycolysis
MyoglobinHighHighLow
Glycogen storesLowIntermediateHigh
Recruitment orderFirstSecondThird
Fatigue rateSlow (resistant)IntermediateFast (fatigable)
Fibre diameterSmallLargeLarge
Mitochondria / capillariesManyManyFew
ColourRedRed–pinkWhite (pale)
Best suited forEndurance, postureSprinting, walkingShort, powerful bursts
Reasoning · structure follows fuel

Every row of that table falls out of §0. A Type I fibre runs aerobically, so it is packed with the machinery aerobic respiration needs — many mitochondria, dense capillaries, and myoglobin (which is red, hence "red muscle") to store and shuttle O₂. That makes it fatigue-resistant but slow, ideal for posture and endurance. A Type IIb fibre runs on anaerobic glycolysis, so it hoards glycogen but skimps on mitochondria and capillaries — pale ("white muscle"), explosively fast, and quick to fatigue as lactate builds. Type IIa sits in between. Colour, capillary density and fatigue-resistance aren't separate facts to memorise — they are all consequences of which energy system the fibre is built around.

Nature vs nurture

Your proportion of fast- vs slow-twitch fibres is mainly determined by genetics — Plate 3.1 shows how a sprinter's quadriceps skew fast-twitch while a marathoner's skew slow. That's nature: suitability for a particular sport. But nurture matters too — training can shift the relative proportions by up to ~10% and increase fibre diameter, while diet (more carbohydrate = more glycogen) tops up the stores.

Label Key — reading the athletes
Power athletes (jumper, sprinter, weightlifter)
Skewed toward fast-twitch — explosive, high-force, fatigable fibres.
Endurance athletes (swimmer, marathoner)
Skewed toward slow-twitch — fatigue-resistant, aerobic fibres.
Average (male)
A roughly even mix — the untrained baseline the athletes diverge from.

Performance & training

Increased stimulation drives hypertrophy — and note the subtlety: hypertrophy means more myofibrils within each fibre, not more fibres. It also brings more PCr, stored glycogen, stored triglyceride and mitochondrial enzymes. Plate 3.2 shows the strength gain from resistance training against no load.

Label Key — the training curve
Resistive training
Strength climbs steeply then plateaus near +30% over ~10 weeks.
No-load training
Flat at 0% — load, not just movement, is what drives adaptation.
Optimal regimen
≈ 6 near-maximal contractions × 3 sets, 3 days/week (progressive overload).
Clinical / real-world · why strength training is prescribed

Progressive-overload strength training — lifting against steadily increasing resistance — pays off well beyond sport. Its benefits read like a preventive-medicine list: ↑ muscle strength → ↓ back injuries; ↑ bone strength → ↓ osteoporosis and fractures; ↑ basal metabolic rate → ↓ weight gain. Because the loaded muscle also pulls on bone, resistance training is one of the few interventions that strengthens the skeleton itself — which is exactly why it's recommended across the lifespan, not just to athletes.

Memory hook · the fibre types

Type I = "I run all day" (slow, red, aerobic, endurance). Type II = "too fast to last" (fast, IIb white/fatigable). One slow marathoner, one white sprinter.

R Recall checklist — fibre types & performance
  • Type I slow oxidative — red, many mitochondria/capillaries, fatigue-resistant, endurance.
  • Type IIa fast oxidative-glycolytic — red-pink, intermediate, sustained power.
  • Type IIb fast glycolytic — white, few mitochondria, fatigable, powerful bursts.
  • Nature — proportion is mostly genetic (suits a sport); nurture — training shifts it ~10% + ↑ diameter.
  • Hypertrophy = more myofibrils per fibre (not more fibres) + more PCr/glycogen/mitochondria.
  • Strength training — ↑ muscle & bone strength & BMR ⇒ ↓ injuries, osteoporosis, weight gain.
